body.en: A differential equation relates a function to its rate of change; separable equations integrate directly.
Write \( \tfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y) \) as \( \tfrac{1}{g(y)}\,dy=f(x)\,dx \) and integrate both sides; an initial condition fixes the constant.

question.en: Solve the separable DE \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{x+1}{y}\) given \(y=2\) when \(x=0\).

caption.en: Direction field for the differential equation dy/dx = (x+1)/y showing the particular solution curve passing through (0, 2).

label.en: ⚠️ Cambridge 9709 Traps — Timing of Constant of Integration & Modulus in Logs

body.en:
Immediate Constant of Integration: The arbitrary constant \(+C\) must be added at the exact line of integration, never tacked on at the end of subsequent algebraic simplification! Integrating \(\int \frac{1}{y}dy = \int k\,dt\) gives \(\ln|y| = kt + C \implies y = e^{kt+C} = Ae^{kt}\). Writing \(\ln y = kt \implies y = e^{kt} + C\) is mathematically invalid and earns zero marks for subsequent work.

Rates of Decay in Word Problems: When formulating a differential equation, words like 'rate of decrease' or 'decay' require an explicit negative sign: \(\frac{dV}{dt} = -k\sqrt{V}\) where \(k > 0\). Omitting the negative turns decay into exponential explosion.

question.en: The temperature \(\theta\) of a cooling metal rod satisfies \(\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -k(\theta - 20)\), where \(t\) is time in minutes and \(k\) is a constant. Given \(\theta = 80\) when \(t = 0\) and \(\theta = 50\) when \(t = 10\), find the value of \(t\) when \(\theta = 30\).

solution.en:
Separate variables and integrate:

\[\int \frac{1}{\theta - 20}\,d\theta = -\int k\,dt \implies \ln(\theta - 20) = -kt + C\]

Apply initial condition \(t = 0, \theta = 80\):

\[\ln(60) = C \implies \ln\left(\frac{\theta - 20}{60}\right) = -kt \implies \theta - 20 = 60e^{-kt}\]

Apply condition \(t = 10, \theta = 50\):

\[30 = 60e^{-10k} \implies e^{-10k} = \frac{1}{2} \implies k = \frac{\ln 2}{10} \approx 0.06931\]

Set \(\theta = 30\):

\[10 = 60e^{-kt} \implies e^{-kt} = \frac{1}{6} \implies t = \frac{\ln 6}{k} = \frac{10\ln 6}{\ln 2} \approx 25.8\text{ minutes}\]
